You will learn to

Prepared by Olimov Azamat

1

Reading · we were nearly there

1.1 Discuss. What is the worst journey you have ever had? What went wrong?

KEY WORDS

a delay when something happens later than planned

to break down to stop working (a car, a bus)

a lift a free ride in somebody's car

a platform where you stand to get on a train

We Were Nearly There

We asked readers for the journey they still talk about. Here are three.

THE WRONG PLATFORM. I was travelling to my cousin's wedding and I was already late. The train was standing at platform six, so I ran, and I got on just as the doors were closing. I was feeling extremely pleased with myself. Then I looked up. Everybody in the carriage was wearing football shirts. Platform six was going north; my wedding was two hundred kilometres south. I arrived in time for the photographs, which my aunt still mentions.

THE HELPFUL STRANGER. Our coach broke down at eleven at night, on a mountain road, in October. While we were waiting for another one, a farmer stopped and asked what was happening. He then drove eleven of us, in three trips, to a village twenty minutes away, where his wife was already making tea. He refused money. When we were leaving the next morning, he was standing at the gate as if he did this every week. Perhaps he does.

THE PUSH. Our coach was climbing a small hill outside the city when it simply stopped. The driver tried three times, then turned round and asked the passengers to get out and push. Nobody laughed. Forty of us — including two men in suits who were going to a conference, and a woman who was carrying a cake — got out and pushed a coach up a hill at eight in the morning. It started. We all got back on. The driver said nothing at all for the next two hours.

Three journeys, then, and only one of them was anybody's fault. The strange thing is that nobody sends us the journeys that went well.

2

Grammar · past continuous

PRESENTATION

The past continuous is a longer action in the past, usually interrupted by a shorter one in the past simple.

form was / were + verb + -ing. It was raining. · All the other passengers were waiting for me. · Negative: It wasn't raining. · Question: Was it raining?

→ The long one starts first. I was reading my book when a flight attendant spoke to me. The reading started first; the speaking interrupted it.

A Sometimes the long action STOPS because of the short one. I was running for the bus when my bag opened. The running stopped.

B Sometimes it CONTINUES afterwards. I was reading my book when she spoke to me. She spoke; the reading carried on.

! Two long actions together — both continuous. While I was waiting, he was making tea.

when usually goes with the past simple; while usually goes with the past continuous. …when the turbulence started. · While I was waiting…

Past simple — the short, finished action

Past continuous — the longer background

I got on the train.

The doors were closing.

The coach broke down.

We were travelling through the mountains.

A flight attendant spoke to me.

I was reading my book.

Did you miss the train?

Were you running for it?

ERROR WARNING

Four things go wrong, and the first two account for most of them:

1 Past simple where you need the background. I read my book when she spoke to me. ✗ → I was reading my book when she spoke to me. ✓ The first version means you read it after she spoke.

2 Past continuous for the short action. The coach was breaking down. ✗ → The coach broke down. ✓ Breaking down takes a second, not an hour.

3 was with they, were with he. They was waiting ✗ → They were waiting ✓ · He were driving ✗ → He was driving ✓

4 State verbs. I was knowing the answer ✗ → I knew the answer ✓. know · want · like · understand · need have no continuous form here either.

Vocabulary · travel collocations

PRESENTATION

The journey, from start to finish:

set off (start a journey) → board a train or plane (get on) → take off (leave by plane) → land (arrive by plane) → change at a station (get off one and on another) → get to a place (arrive)

Two more: travel around a country (visit many places in it) · hitchhike (stand by the road and ask for free rides) · give somebody a lift (drive them where they are going)

When it goes wrong: miss a train · your car breaks down · there is turbulence during the flight · you have an accident · you get stuck in a traffic jam · there is something wrong with the plane · there is a strike · you get lost · there is a long queue · there is a delay

Careful: you miss a train, you do not lose it. And take off is what the plane does, not the passenger.

PRONUNCIATION — WAS AND WERE

In positives and questions they are weak. It was raining → /wəz/. · We were driving → /wə/. · Were we driving fast? → /wə/. You barely hear them.

In negatives they are strong. It WASN'T raining → /wɒznt/. · We WEREN'T driving fast → /wɜːnt/.

So the negative is the loud one, which is the opposite of what students expect. If you hear a clear, stressed word there, it is almost certainly wasn't or weren't.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

was and were almost vanish. I was reading → /aɪwəzriːdɪŋ/ — one weak sound between two stressed ones. Students hear reading and write the present.

And was joins to what follows. was a → /wəzə/ · were all → /wərɔːl/ · was in → /wəzɪn/. Listen for the -ing; the auxiliary will be in front of it whether you hear it or not.

5

Writing · a travel blog

LISTENING INTO WRITING

First, listen to Lucila, who is flying from Peru to Australia for six months, talking to her friend Katie, who already lives in Sydney.

5.1 Listen and underline the correct answer.

1 Katie will meet Lucila at five / after six o'clock.

2 They will meet at the airport / train station.

3 When Katie arrived in Sydney she was too tired to enjoy / excited by the view.

4 Katie's home town is similar to / different from Sydney.

5 Lucila will stay with Katie for her whole trip / a short time.

LINKING WORDS

Five small words hold a blog together. Each one does a different job:

and — adds a similar idea. They were very friendly and welcoming.

but — adds a different idea. Some of them are expensive, but most are really cheap.

so — gives the result. I slept most of the way, so I'm not tired.

because — gives the reason. You can't bring fresh fruit because it could carry diseases.

when — two things at the same time, or one just after the other. When I got off the plane, the first thing I noticed was how organised everything is.

so and because are opposites. It was raining, so we stayed in. · We stayed in because it was raining. Same facts, opposite order. Getting them the wrong way round is the commonest mistake in this lesson.

5.2 Put and, but, so, because or when where you see ▲.

1 We were very tired, we went straight to bed.

2 we got to the hotel, I unpacked.

3 It was the middle of the night, the streets were completely empty.

4 The restaurant looked small and cheap, the food was amazing.

5 We gave the waiter twenty dollars the service was excellent.

6 We ran into a shopping centre the storm began.

7 We went to the National Museum we wanted to understand the country's history.

8 We tried to check in, we were very early and the desk was closed.

5.3 Join each pair twice — once with so, once with because.

1 It was raining. We stayed in the hotel. →

2 The train was cancelled. We took a taxi. →

5.4 Read the model blog entry, then answer.

MODEL · TUESDAY, 7 NOVEMBER

SYDNEY — FIRST EVENING

I've arrived, and it's amazing! It was a long flight, but I slept most of the way, so I'm not tired. Katie was right — the view from the plane was spectacular.

When I got off the plane, the first thing I noticed was how organised everything is. There are signs everywhere that tell you where to go and what to do. There are a lot of rules about bringing food into Australia. You can't bring in fresh fruit because it could carry diseases that are dangerous for plants here.

It was really easy to find the train and get to the city centre. Katie was waiting for me at Central Station — it was wonderful to see her again.

Katie lives in a lovely old house with two housemates. They were very friendly and welcoming, and they don't mind if I stay until I find my own place. We all had a lovely dinner together, but after that I felt very tired. In fact, I'm finding it difficult to keep my eyes open and write this, so I'll finish now — more tomorrow.
